title: Dinner with the team lead
hook: You said no to dinner. Now he's gone cold.

n1.text:
Week three of your internship. It's 6:40 p.m. and the office is emptying. Your team lead stops at your desk. He signs off on your review.
Vikram: You're doing well. Let's get dinner tonight, just us. I'll tell you how things really work here.

choices.label: "Thank you, but I need to get home. Could we do coffee in the office tomorrow?"
choices.consequence:
Vikram: Hm. Sure.
His face closes a little. He walks off without saying bye.
choices.expert_note: You kept the professional part and dropped the part that felt off: after hours, alone. Offering office hours is a fair counter.

choices.label: Go. You can't afford to annoy him.
choices.consequence: Dinner is mostly fine. A lot of personal questions. He insists on dropping you home. You get in at eleven feeling like you were at work for five extra hours you couldn't leave.
choices.expert_note: When someone controls your review, your room to choose gets squeezed. Going doesn't mean you were okay with it.

choices.label: "Sorry, I have plans tonight."
choices.consequence:
Vikram: Tomorrow, then.
He says it like it's settled.
choices.expert_note: An excuse buys you tonight, and that is often the right move in the moment. The invitation usually comes back.

n2.text:
Over the next few days, something shifts. You're dropped from a client call. Your messages get "ok." and nothing more. At the coffee machine, a colleague lowers her voice.
Sneha: Did something happen with Vikram? He gets like this when people say no to his dinners.

choices.label: "Wait. It's not just me?"
choices.consequence: Sneha tells you she started CC'ing another senior on everything and saving his messages. "It didn't fix him. It covered me."
choices.expert_note: Learning it's a pattern changes the question from "what did I do?" to "what does he do?" Other people's experience is information.

choices.label: "No, no. All fine."
choices.consequence:
Sneha: Okay. If it isn't, tell me.
You go back to your desk, alone with it.
choices.expert_note: Saying nothing is a way of protecting yourself when you don't know who's safe. The door she opened is still there.

choices.label: Start writing down dates and what was said
choices.consequence: It feels dramatic. A week later, when you can't remember which day the call was, you're glad you did.
choices.expert_note: Notes with dates are quiet power. You may never use them. They turn a feeling into a record.

n3.text: Friday. HR sends the mid-internship feedback form. One box reads: "Anything about your work environment you'd like to share?" Your college also has an internship coordinator. Five weeks to go.

choices.label: Write what happened in the form. Just the facts.
choices.consequence: You write four plain sentences with dates. Your finger hovers. You press submit.
choices.expert_note: Facts and dates, no adjectives. Putting it on record means it no longer lives only in your head.

choices.label: Leave it blank. Talk to your college coordinator instead.
choices.consequence: You book ten minutes with her on Monday and tell her all of it.
choices.expert_note: When the person with power is the problem, someone outside that line of power can do things you can't.

choices.label: Leave it blank. Keep your head down for five weeks.
choices.consequence: You type "N/A" and close the tab.
choices.expert_note: Getting through it is a legitimate goal. Not reporting doesn't mean it didn't happen or didn't matter.

end_a.title: On record
end_a.text: HR replies: "Noted, thank you." Nothing visible changes. Vikram stays curt. Two weeks later you're moved to Sneha's project and nobody says why.
end_a.takeaway: Power makes saying no feel risky. Putting things on record is one way to share that risk.

end_b.title: Someone outside
end_b.text: She listens without interrupting. "You're not the first from that company." She offers to move you, or to check in every week. You stay, with the weekly call.
end_b.takeaway: When the problem is the person in charge, look for someone outside their reach.

end_c.title: Five weeks
end_c.text: You finish the internship. The letter is lukewarm. You still think you were right to say no. You also wish it hadn't cost you anything.
end_c.takeaway: Saying no to someone with power over you can cost something. That cost is on them, not you.
